MN202611_ltv3tdrr3j.t:
Inteko y'Umuco yakoze ubushakashatsi ahitwa mu Twicarabami twa Nyaruteja, basanga ari amateka y’ukuri yabayeho mu bihe byo hambere.

André Ntagwabira Umushakashatsi Ushinzwe Amateka ashingiye ku Bisigaratongo asobanura ko Nyaruteja yari isanzwe ari iteme riri kuri Nyabarongo, rigahuza Kigali na Nduga.

Icyo gihe Umwami Semugeshi yerekanaga ko azambukira i Nyaruteja akigarurira u Burundi nk’uko Abanyarwanda bambukiye kuri Nyaruteja yindi bakigarurira i Nduga.

I Nyaruteja ni mu Ntara y’Amajyepfo, Akarere ka Gisagara, Umurenge wa Nyanza, Akagari ka Higiro, Umudugudu w’Akabakene, ahahoze ari mu Mvejuru. Izina rya Nyaruteja ni izina ryatanzwe n’Umwami Mutara I Semugeshi ku buryo bw’umutsindo ugamije kwigarurira u Burundi.

Ati “Abami b’u Rwanda bakundaga kwita uduce tumwe na tumwe two ku nkiko amazina asanzwe mu Gihugu mu rwego rw’imitsindo”.

Aha muri Nyaruteja hari urugo rwa Rwabugiri i Ngeri, nyuma haje kuba n'urugo rw'umuhungu we witwaga Muhigirwa wategekaga umutwe w'ingabo z'Inyaruguru.

Ku Ngoma ya Mutara I Semugeshi ni ho habaye amasezerano agamije guhosha amakimbirane hagati y’u Rwanda n’u Burundi. Igihe u Rwanda rwigaruriraga u Bungwe ku ngoma ya Ruganzu II Ndori, rwahise rugera ku marembo y’u Burundi bwatwarwaga na Mutaga II Nyamubi.

Ibihugu byombi byaharaniraga urubibi aho i Nyaruteja ku ruhande rw’u Rwanda, cyangwa se i Ngozi ku ruhande rw’u Burundi.

Kuva ubwo hagati y’u Rwanda n’u Burundi, habaye intambara zidashira. Izi ntambara zashoboraga kuba bugacya zongeye, ahanini ugasanga zarabaga zigamije kwirata ubutwari, buri ruhande rudashaka kwemera ko abandi babarusha imbaraga.

Ibi bitero ariko akenshi byakurikirwaga no kunyaga; ari ukunyaga ubutaka cyangwa amatungo ku ruhande rwabaga rwatsinze. Izi ntambara z’urudaca zaje kurambirana, bigera aho umwami w’u Rwanda ndetse n’umwami w’u Burundi biyemeza guhurira aho i Nyaruteja, bagirana imimaro (amasezerano), biyemeza kutazongera guterana ukundi.

Mu bindi byatumye haba aya masezerano, ni uko umwami w’u Rwanda Mutara I Semugeshi yifuzaga kumenya birambuye iby’inzira y’ishora yagaragaraga mu bwiru bw’Abarundi. Mu gutegura uko Semugeshi yazahura n’umwami w’u Burundi Mutaga II Nyamubi, intumwa z’impande zombi zabanje kugendererana.

Nyuma abami bombi bahurira i Nyaruteja, bagirana imimaro, kuva ubwo hitwa mu Twicarabami twa Nyaruteja.

Mutara I Semugeshi na Mutaga II Nyamubi baranywanye ndetse bemeranywa ko u Rwanda n’u Burundi bitazongera gushotorana. Iyi mimaro kandi yasobanuraga ko niba u Rwanda ruteye ikindi gihugu, u Burundi budashobora kuba bwatabara icyo gihugu cyatewe.

Ibi akaba ari na ko byagombaga kuba mu gihe u Burundi buteye ikindi gihugu. Ibi byari bihereye ku buryo Ruganzu II Ndori yari yaratabaye u Bugesera, bigatuma u Burundi butabasha kubwigarurira. Nyuma y’aya masezerano, u Burundi bwateye u Bugesera burabwigarurira.

Muri aya masezerano, u Rwanda na rwo rwungukiyemo inzira nshya y’Ubwiru ari yo nzira y’ishora Umwami Semugeshi yifuzaga kumenya cyane. Umwami w’u Burundi yoherereje uw’u Rwanda umwiru witwa Nyamwonda mwene Burenge kugira ngo yigishe abiru b’Abanyarwanda ibijyanye n’inzira y’ishora, ndetse anategure bwa mbere imihango igendana na yo.

Abiru b’Abanyarwanda bamaze gutora ibijyanye n’ubu bwiru, ndetse n’ubwiru bumaze gutunganywa neza ngo bujyane n’iby’u Rwanda nko gusimbuza amazina y’udusozi tw’i Burundi amazina yo mu Rwanda, ubwo nibwo imihango yatangiye.

Amasezerano yongeye kuvugururwa n’Umwami Kigeri IV Rwabugiri w’u Rwanda hamwe na Mwezi IV Gisabo w’u Burundi. Mu kuvugurura ayo maszerano ariko, abami bombi ntibahuye nk’uko byari byaragenze mu Twicarabami, ahubwo bohereje ababahagararira bagaragiwe n’abandi batware n’ingabo, bahurira ahitwa mu Ryagisegenya.

Igihe amasezerano yavugurwaga, Umwami Kigeri IV Rwabugiri yari mu rugo rwe rwari i Ngeri muri Nyaruguru. Aha hantu rero bahuriye niho hitwa mu Twicarabami twa Nyaruteja kuva icyo gihe kugeza na nubu niko hakitwa.

Aha mu Twicarabami twa Nyaruteja rero hari mu hantu nyaburanga hagomba kubungwabungwa kuko hafite ayo mateka yihariye yaho.

MN202611_hwovrehs88.t:
Bola Tinubu (in red hat) would be 79 at the end of a second term, if he is re-elected

Abdulhadi Dalhatu is something of a rarity in Nigeria politics.

At 38, he is among the young people seeking elected office in a country where about 80% of the population is under 40.

He hopes his age will stand in his favour as he campaigns for a seat in the state assembly in the northern Kano state in January's general elections.

"Younger people are the majority in this country and should be deciding the future," Dalhatu tells the BBC.

But Nigeria's political history suggests he faces an uphill battle.

Since the return to civilian rule in 1999, Goodluck Jonathan has been the youngest person elected president, taking office at the age of 53.

The current president, Bola Tinubu, is 74 and would be 79 by the end of a second term if he is re-elected in January.

His main challengers are also considerably older. Atiku Abubakar, seeking the presidency for the seventh time, is 79, while Peter Obi is 65.

Of the 18 presidential candidates, only one is under 40 - Moses Olusoji Adebisi, a 35-year-old businessman representing the Democratic Leadership Alliance (DLA).

Although he says he is confident of winning, few Nigerians appear to know much about him and he has not been seen much on the campaign trail.

The contrast is striking in a country with one of the world's youngest populations, where young people have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to shape political debate and mobilise for change.

In the previous election, Obi, then 61, galvanised millions of young Nigerians through a social media-driven movement known as the "Obedients".

His campaign promised a break from the established political order, appealing particularly to young people struggling to find jobs and earn a decent living.

But his failure to win the presidency left many of his supporters disillusioned.

"At the time we were so hopeful, but unfortunately the result wasn't what we wanted, which made many lose hope in the system," former Obedient Nonso Chukwudi tells the BBC.

The movement had built on the momentum of the EndSars protests in 2020, which grew into one of Nigeria's biggest youth-led movement in decades.

Initially sparked by anger over police brutality, the demonstrators developed into a wider call for political reform, accountability and greater youth participation in governance.

But the protests were eventually crushed by the authorities. About 56 were reportedly killed, although officials dispute this figure, while hundreds were arrested and some had their bank accounts frozen.

Both EndSars and the Obedients demonstrated the capacity of young Nigerians to mobile around political causes.

Abdulhadi Dalhatu hopes to be president one day but bemoans the financial obstacles needed to contest

But turning that enthusiasm into sustained electoral participation has proved much harder.

Hajara Musa, 33, is among those who have lost faith in the political system. She has no plans to register or vote in the near future.

"I just feel like things are already determined and I'll just be wasting my time. It is going to be the same people all over again," she tells the BBC.

The electoral register appears to reflect this growing disillusionment.

Although the number of registered voters has increased by 10 million to over 103 million since the last election, enrolment of those under 35 has actually fallen, by about seven million.

Young people now account for just 29% of registered voters, down from 40% in 2023.

Nigeria's electoral commission, Inec, says it has made efforts to encourage more young people to register ahead of the 2027 general elections.

This includes appointing nine ambassadors from the entertainment industry, spanning film, music and comedy, to reach younger audiences.

But the figures suggest these efforts have yet to make a significant difference.

Dalhatu says he understands the frustration but argues that young Nigerians cannot expect change, if they stay away from the political process.

"Unfortunately, many prefer to just post on social media" instead of getting involved, he says.

Of course being young does not mean you are necessarily the best candidate.

For those who want to participate, there is a formidable obstacle to getting into politics - money.

Young people now account for just 29% of registered voters, down from 40% in 2023

Dalhatu dreams of becoming president one day, but says he has previously had to abandon campaigns because he could not raise enough funds.

The cost of running for office in Nigeria is notoriously high.

Under the Electoral Act, presidential candidates were allowed to spend up to 5bn naira (£2.8m; $3.7m) on campaigns ahead of the 2023 elections. That spending limit has since been doubled.

The cost of nomination forms alone puts the presidency beyond the reach of most aspiring young Nigerians.

The ruling All Progressive Congress (APC), along with the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the African Democratic Congress (ADC) have each set their presidential nomination fee at 100m naira ($74,000; £56,000), making it extremely hard for new challengers to emerge.

Since the return to democracy in 1999, only two parties have governed Nigeria - the PDP from 1999 to 2015 and the APC since 2015.

These parties, alongside the ADC, formed last year by politicians who had defected from the other two, have established nationwide network of branches, supporters and campaigners.

Those aspiring candidates without the financial resources to secure nomination forms and compete in the internal party contests of the main parties have little chances of becoming president.

The barriers are also evident in the National Assembly.

Not one of Nigeria's 109 senators is under 40, while only 14 of the 360 members of the House of Representatives fall into that age group.

"I have been in politics for many years and I will tell you that young people in this country lack the resources to become president," says Dalhatu, who is running under Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.

Atiku Abubakar is seeking the presidency for a seventh time

Fatima Zahra Umar, a young politician in the APC who has previously tried to run for a seat in the House of Representatives, agrees.

"Young Nigerians are poor. Nigerian politics is cash-intensive, so participation is guided by money," she says, adding that young people are often content with having a bit of influence as a special advisor to a senior politician.

But political analyst Seun Ajayi believes the problems go beyond the financial barriers.

"We have some of the most brilliant young persons in the world, but they are either not interested in politics or feel satisfied when given a small role in government," he says.

"The old men are not going to sit idle and allow us to push them out. We have to fight for the big positions, but at the moment I don't see the zeal."

Umar believes changing attitudes towards young leadership is equally important.

"Culturally, we are not primed to trust or accept the brilliance of a younger person, so it will be very difficult," she says.

"Old men are still holding on to the system."

Some Nigerians took inspiration from the wave of success of young candidates in the recent midterm elections in the US, some of whom have roots in Africa.

"America Has Done It, Can Nigerians Do the Same?" entertainer Charly Boy wrote on X, in a post that was widely shared.

He said the US results served as a warning to Nigerian politicians that no matter how powerful the political machine, voters can change the direction of government.

He called on young people to interrogate candidates about their past promises: "Has life improved? Where are the jobs, security and affordable living?

"Democracy is not a spectator sport, nor is it about sharing rice," he wrote.

MN202611_azezxg7wea.t:
Landon Tresp, 16, left, met the girl playing Among Us before alerting his mother, Khristina, 41, to the missing teen's predicament

Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when he began chatting on his laptop with another player.

She was also a teenager, and the pair "kind of just clicked," he tells the BBC.

He told her he liked her name, and she confessed that it was an alias. She was a runaway, she said - and was being held against her will, hundreds of miles from home, though she didn't know exactly where. The girl, 17, and had been missing for more than a year.

Stunned, Landon felt "helpless," he says - and, after learning more details over two weeks of chatting, he decided to tell his mother, Khristina on 31 October this year. The 41-year-old nurse and mother of five was putting Halloween makeup on her younger children for trick-or-treating when he briefed her.

That set the mother and son on a path to track down his friend, contact her mother, cooperate with the FBI - and ultimately witness the rescue of the teen - only 24 hours after Landon first alerted Khristina to her plight.

"She had one opportunity to reach out her hand and ask for help, and she chose me," Khristina says of the girl, who was 15 when she went missing.

A screenshot shows Khristina on a call with the girl as she showed her the knife her alleged captor kept under his pillow

The Tresps have shared with BBC screenshots of communication with the girl and a photo matching the criminal complaint to corroborate their story.

Landon first told his mother about "Jenny" - whose identity the BBC is protecting - in mid-October, a few weeks before the rescue.

"He had mentioned something about maybe a week or so into talking to her that he met a girl online, and she was really sweet," says Khristina - who cautioned him that "you don't always know who's on the other side of the screen".

"She's just having a really hard time and looking for a friend," he told her.

But Landon was becoming increasingly concerned as Jenny told him more about her situation.

They'd met playing Among Us, a game Landon describes as "kind of like online space Clue".

After telling Landon that she was a runaway, "Jenny" said an older man had taken her across state lines and wouldn't let her leave. She was the subject of a missing person investigation, and she sent Landon links to stories about her disappearance. But she believed police were no longer looking for her.

Jenny was scared and desperate, and that's why Landon went to his mother.

Her maternal instincts on high alert, Khristina contacted Jenny herself on Discord, the encrypted platform.

During the conversation, Khristina said she told the Colorado mother how she'd been through "years of abuse in her life and lots and lots of problems".

Within hours, Jenny started calling Khristina "mama".

Among Us supports cross platform play online with 4-15 players on various devices

The Colorado mother knew things were serious when she read the missing persons articles. Jenny knew she was in Oregon and gave the name of a city, but she didn't know where she was being held exactly. Khristina knew she needed more. She told Jenny to find a piece of mail or another document in the house that had a full name on it, which the girl did.

"That's when I went to work," Khristina says, delving into tax and property records.

Khristina narrowed down addresses, then searched them on a real estate site to find pictures. She showed the photos to Jenny, who confirmed that the second one was where she was being held.

The "next thing she asked me was to please not tell anyone until [her captor] was gone - that he did have weapons in the house and she was very scared," Khristina said.

Jenny promised Khristina she'd call her back through the game platform when he left the next morning, and in the meantime Khristina began looking for the law enforcement agency that had been assigned to the missing teen's case. She contacted Jenny's mother on social media, spoke briefly to her on the phone and then got a call from an FBI agent.

"Have you seen her alive?'" the agent asked Khristina.

"And I said: 'I have; I video chatted with her, I've seen her, and she goes 'Oh my God, I cannot believe any of this'," Khristina recalled.

When Jenny called Khristina back after her alleged captor left home, the FBI monitored their conversation. According to the criminal complaint's record of the conversation, Jenny explained how she'd met Adam Hunter Harmel on social media in May 2025.

He'd told her he was disabled and his hips were "messed up," offering Jenny money if she'd help get him to Oregon.

After he picked her up in Utah, however, Harmel threw her phone into a river, drove her to Oregon and kept her in the basement. He forced her to sleep against the wall in his bed, with a knife under his pillow, to prevent her from escaping. He gave Jenny a cell phone with no ability to make calls, but it could connect to wifi, which is how she played the online game.

The 39-year-old "would become violent and aggressive", the document says, which included hitting her and sexually assaulting her.

He also allegedly forced Jenny to remove her braces with pliers so she wouldn't be identifiable.

As Khristina and the FBI heard all of this, law enforcement were staging to bring Jenny to safety, after being alerted to her whereabouts.

While Harmel was out of the home, officers were sent to the street and the address, and Khristina was prepping Jenny for her run to freedom.

She'd unsuccessfully tried escaping before, she told Khristina.

Law enforcement was "phenomenal…giving me an update, you know, 'We're nine minutes out, we're seven minutes out,'" says Khristina, who was on the phone with Jenny the entire time, her son Landon watching at her side.

Khristina could hear other people in the home with Jenny, and she was afraid that someone would catch wind of what was happening and harm the girl.

But she kept any of those fears from Jenny.

"I want you to take three deep breaths with me," she told the teen. "When an officer tells me to go, and I relay that message to you, I want you to run up those stairs as fast as you can … Grab that basement door.

"I want you to keep going down that hallway and grab that front door… do not stop.'"

The mother and son watched breathlessly as Jenny ran into the arms of a state trooper.

Harmel is now in federal custody and has been charged in a criminal complaint with transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. Local Oregon media also reported he'd been accused of sexually abusing a six-year-old in the months before Jenny disappeared - and a sexual abuse protective order was granted against him in March 2025.

A lawyer for the defendant did not respond to a BBC request for comment.

Jenny, meanwhile, remains in daily communication with Khristina and Landon - who still enjoys playing online games with her.

"Sometimes we just sit on video chat, just so she knows she has someone that cares," Khristina says. "She was on video last night when I cooked dinner …it's nice to know that when she has a bad day or a bad moment, she can call me right away or call Landon right away."

"She's doing great for what she's gone through."

They haven't met in person yet, but they're in the process of trying to make that happen.

"I hope I can put my arms around her soon," Khristina says.

Will COP31 end with a new global climate deal?

Talks were set to resume at the UN COP31 summit on Sunday for a second day of overtime as countries struggle to reach a new global climate deal.

Nations were deadlocked in Turkey on how to advance the fight against global warming, after new draft agreements included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.

A third and "final" text was sent to delegates in the early hours of Sunday morning and members had until 06:00 local time (0300 GMT) to raise concerns before a 9am local time (0600GMT) meeting for approval.

If countries cannot reach consensus - as required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended to reconvene next year.

A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels, but a second, pared-down version released Thursday stripped away all mentions of coal, oil and gas - sparking threats of a walk out.

The fallout led to the summit in Antalya blowing past the original deadline of Friday . On Saturday negotiating teams who had Sunday morning flights were rescheduling them - a sign a deal was still not in sight, and raising the risk that as teams eventually had to leave, the meeting could lose the critical numbers needed to pass an agreement.

As part of a last ditch effort to produce an acceptable text, the European Union and Saudi Arabia - who were deeply divided over the future of fossil fuels - were brought together on Saturday to seek a compromise.

COP31 President Murat Kurum says he believes the third version of the text sent to delegates addresses outlying concerns.

COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum told delegates in the early hours of Sunday morning he believed concerns had been addressed.

"We ask you to look at this decision carefully," Kurum said.

"We are closer than ever to agreement on the remaining issues."

If the countries can't agree, the summit would end with no deal and be reconvened next year.

This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.

Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU were fighting to have a commitment to move away from fossil fuels put back into the final agreement, after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.

"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.

Tuvalu's Climate Minister Maina Talia told reporters it was a "red line" for the low-lying Pacific nation: "We're talking about the root cause of all of this".

Panama's Minister of Environment Juan Carlos Navarro says it is not acceptable for a COP agreement not to mention fossil fuels.

France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut, took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture - a technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground.

She said it was being used as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.

"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.

For the first time at a COP, the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal set under the Paris climate accord of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.

The world is entering a period called "overshoot".

Beyond this point scientists warn millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.

COP31 President of Negotiations, Chris Bowen, says the summit should focus on the shift towards clean energy.

But Australia's Climate Change and Energy Minister, Chris Bowen, who is leading negotiations, pushed back on the need to include language on fossil fuels.

He argued the summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.

Another key issues raised by developing nations is the the lack of money.

Another sticking point involved a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptations to climate change, however the EU has previously said it would not support this.

Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (£91bn) by 2035 - a figure that was then removed.

"We did not come here to beg, we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.

Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.

"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.

Perezida wa Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky yashyigikiye ibitero byinshi igihugu cye cyagabye ku iteme ry'ingenzi cyane rihuza Uburusiya n'akarere ka Crimea bwigaruriye, abyita "igisubizo kiboneye" ku bitero 109 binyuranye Uburusiya bwagabye ku mateme yo muri Ukraine.

Mu magambo yabwiriye BBC i Kyiv, Zelensky yavuze ko ibitero bikaze Uburusiya bwagabye kuri Ukraine byakurikiye ibitero Ukraine yagabye ku iteme rya Crimea, ari gusa "ikimenyetso cyuko [Perezida w'Uburusiya] Vladimir Putin adashaka kurekeraho. Arashaka impamvu yatuma akaza umurego".

Yahakanye ibivugwa na Perezida w'Uburusiya ko iryo teme – rihuza Uburusiya n'uwo mwigimbakirwa Uburusiya bwiyometseho mu 2014 mu buryo bunyuranyije n'amategeko – ryakoreshwaga "gusa n'abasivile".

Yagize ati: "Hari ibimenyetso, si amagambo gusa ya Putin. Dushobora kureba."

Perezida wa Ukraine yatanze urugero rw'amafoto yo ku mbuga zo kuri murandasi (internet) agaragaza ibifaru n'ibindi bikoresho bya gisirikare by'Uburusiya birimo kunyura muri uwo muhanda biva mu Burusiya bijya muri Crimea bwigaruriye, nk'ahantu hanyuzwa ibikoresho.

Yagize ati: "Putin abaye akoresha internet, ashobora kubibona."

Perezida wa Ukraine yongeyeho ko Uburusiya bwagabye ibitero bya misile n'iby'indege nto z'intambara zitajyamo umupilote (zizwi nka 'drones') ku mateme yo muri Ukraine.

Ibitero bikomatanye bya misile na 'drone' bya Ukraine byo muri iki cyumweru byashenye igice cyo hagati cy'uwo muhanda wo ku iteme rya Crimea, bituma igice kimwe cyaryo gihirima hamwe na kimwe mu bice birifashe (birishyigikiye) bigwa mu nyanja, ibyo bikaba byaratumye ubu umuhanda wo kuri iryo teme utari nyabagendwa.

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Ibitero by'Uburusiya kuri Ukraine byarakomeje ku mugoroba wo ku wa gatanu no mu ijoro ryo ku wa gatanu rishyira ku wa gatandatu: umuhungu w'imyaka irindwi yiciwe mu bitero bya misile na 'drone' mu mujyi Zelensky avukamo wa Kryvyi Rih, uri mu karere ka Dnipropetrovsk kari rwagati mu gihugu. Abategetsi baho bavuze ko icyo gihe uwo muhungu yari ari mu kibuga cyo gukiniramo.

Umukozi wo kwa muganga w'umugore w'imyaka 20 na we yarishwe. Umutegetsi waho yongeyeho ko ubwo abakora ubutabazi bari bageze aho byabereye, aho hantu hongeye kugabwaho igitero hakoreshejwe 'drones' zikoreshwa na moteri z'indege. Abandi bantu 58 barakomeretse muri uwo mujyi.

Ikigo cya Ukraine gishinzwe gukora ubutabazi bwihuse (DSNS) cyavuze ko abantu 11 na bo bakomeretse mu karere ka Kharkiv kari mu majyaruguru ashyira uburasirazuba bw'igihugu, naho undi muntu umwe arakomereka i Rivne, mu majyaruguru ashyira uburengerazuba bw'icyo gihugu.

Uburusiya bwagabye igitero gisesuye kuri Ukraine kuva muri Gashyantare (2) mu mwaka wa 2022.

Zelensky yabivuze mbere y'inama yagiranye i Kyiv na Minisitiri w'ingabo w'Ubwongereza Wes Streeting, wabwiye Perezida wa Ukraine ko yagiyeyo kugaragaza ko Uburayi bushyize hamwe mu gushyigikira Ukraine.

Streeting yagize ati: "Uko Putin arushaho kugerageza kuducamo ibice, ni ko turushaho kwiyemeza."

Yavuze ko misile z'Uburusiya zarashe muri Pologne ku wa gatanu, mu myitozo ya gisirikare y'ibihugu byo mu ihuriro ryiswe iry'abakorerabushake, ari "ubushotoranyi bukabije".

Streeting yavuze ko igihe ibyo byabereye bigaragara ko "birenze kuba uruhurirane [si impanuka]".

Abajijwe na BBC ku gisubizo cy'umuryango wo gutabarana w'Uburayi n'Amerika (OTAN/NATO), Streeting yavuze ko uburyo bwiza cyane ari "ugukorera Ukraine ibirenzeho" kugira ngo yirwaneho kuri Putin yise "umwicanyi wa nta mpuhwe".

Uko kuntu Streeting yasobanuye Putin guhuye n'amagambo Zelensky yari yavuze mbere, ubwo yavugaga ko Perezida w'Uburusiya ari "umwicanyi". Ibyo yabivuze asubiza Perezida w'Amerika Donald Trump, muri iki cyumweru wise Putin "inshuti" ye.

At least three people have been killed and 36 were still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory in western Java on Saturday.

Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for the missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.

Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.

The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.

Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire.

Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.

"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.

Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.

Firefighters had been called to the building at 1630 local time (0930 GMT) but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.

"When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said.

The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities.

On LinkedIn the company describes itself as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.

Fisher's estuarine moths are highly threatened due to coastal erosion

Wildlife enthusiasts have made a record-breaking number of sightings of an elusive moth at a nature reserve.

The Fisher's estuarine moth has been spotted 111 times at Abbotts Hall in Great Wigborough, near Colchester, in 2026.

Dr Zoe Ringwood, of Essex Wildlife Trust, said work to boost the highly threatened species' population had been an "important success story".

The charity has pledged to continue surveying new and existing plots on the Essex coast.

Fisher's estuarine moths can be recognised by their pale gold-brown wing colour with light and dark spots, and are naturally found in low-lying areas of natural grassland which are vulnerable to erosion.

They are reliant on rare hog's fennel for their survival, but the plant has been affected by rising sea levels.

To protect the species, Essex Wildlife Trust planted hog's fennel at Abbotts Hall in 2005 and introduced moth eggs five years later.

There is now a self-sustaining population of the moth at Abbotts Hall, according to Essex Wildlife Trust

More than 100 of the scarce insect were recorded for the first time in 2025, before the record was broken again in 2026.

The charity said it was confident there was now a self-sustaining population at Abbotts Hall.

"[It is] a reflection of how taking evidence-based conservation action can achieve positive results for a threatened Essex species," said Ringwood, its senior conservation evidence manager.

Hog's fennel has also been planted at nature reserves in Fingringhoe, Wrabness and nearby Tollesbury.

Stepping into a job like Mauricio Pochettino has done at Manchester United , where managers have come and gone frequently, will always lead you to wonder why the others have not lasted very long.

Irrespective of results, you face these first few days in your new post with suspicion.

So, while what happens in Pochettino's first game against Liverpool on Sunday is important, it will not define his early opinions of the club - good or bad.

Whenever you take over a team in mid-season, which I did on a few occasions, you don't usually get much time to work with your players before your first game.

Jumping straight in and going straight to the heart of a two-day preparation for a game, like Pochettino has done before United go to Anfield, is so difficult and I am not sure any manager can honestly make a profound difference.

A change of voice helps, I'm sure, but so does showing strength and confidence in your own principles and making sure the players understand you demand complete and utter commitment in all the games you face, starting with this one.

With time on the training ground being so limited, my initial work would focus on us being a team and working up and down the pitch together, by breaking down different scenarios inside the game and what we should do in them.

I'd keep the focus on hard work and making us difficult to beat - clean sheets are so under-rated.

Then, on the day, your first pre-match speech is always a massive one, and it will be the same for Pochettino too.

My first team talk would always focus on generating an 'us against the world' mentality. As a manager coming in now, you've usually got the job because the team has struggled, so you can play on that to motivate the players.

You can use media reports and stories to show the negativity against them - but then counter that by producing a real 'stand-up and be counted' kind of rallying call, before sending them out on the pitch, while mentioning your faith in them to succeed.

Pochettino had his first training session with United's players on Thursday

I would have selected my team before I met the players, through my own knowledge and also with help from within.

Whichever club I went in at, I'd expect to know something about most of the players within the group in terms of their position and ability, but understanding the character of the squad was vital too.

The existing staff would know more about the lads' qualities in that respect than myself or anyone who had just arrived with me, so I'd always discuss that with the people I had inherited, from fitness coaches to the medical department.

It's what your own eyes tell you that is most important, however. Going into your first game gives you the opportunity to see for yourself what your players are made of - and it can be a completely different view from what other people see.

Most of the early games I managed would be hit and miss in terms of selection, but I would quickly work out the strengths and weaknesses of the group.

As I've mentioned in previous columns, one of my first aims at any club where I was manager was about putting out a team, not a group of individuals.

It does not take long to see when that is not happening. I can remember my first game of my first spell at Stoke, a 4-2 defeat at Walsall in the Championship.

I wasn't universally enamoured by certain crowd favourites in that team and, while any manager knows that leaving some of them out could have an adverse effect on the supporters' view of yourself, you have to stand up and make decisions based on what you see.

It is the same if there are other issues with the squad you have inherited too.

West Brom's first game after I was appointed manager was a draw with West Ham on New Year's Day 2015.

I sat in the stands at Upton Park with my son, Anthony, who was concerned how different the Albion team was compared to Crystal Palace , the last team I had managed in the Premier League.

He was right to worry about it, but we still found a way - a totally different way of playing, but still a way to win that suited the group.

Pulis (far right) watched West Brom play West Ham with (right to left) his son Anthony, his assistant Dave Kemp and the Baggies' technical director, Terry Burton

My initial aims after arriving at any club mid-season were pretty direct and also pretty basic too.

The staff I inherited did not just know the players, they were also the first group who had to understand my objectives and also my principles - like the work ethic I expected, for example.

Irrespective of what they were used to doing, it was imperative they followed my lead.

One of the clubs I arrived at were struggling at the foot of the table and also suffering from a glut of injuries.

In my opinion, the players were taking advantage of a very honest and hard-working medical department, who were quite accommodating on the treatment times for the lads.

I changed that immediately, so injured players were treated at 9am, 2pm and 4pm, with sessions in-between those times for strength and recovery workouts.

This did not go down well with the players because it impeded on their social lives and, in one case, a player whose injury record was not exactly brilliant came to me complaining that his wife expected him to pick his children up from school and being asked to be in at 4pm affected his private life too.

I did not budge, and funnily enough the player in question recovered quite quickly - as did the majority of the other injured players.

Pulis at work on the training ground with West Brom in 2015

Asking injured players to be at the training ground all day was by far the best way of getting them fit, in my experience, and the medical departments I managed were all working well past 4pm anyway so it was no hardship to them.

Just on that side of things, I would sometimes get the feeling some medical departments thought that, if they weren't treating players, then they weren't doing their jobs.

That was completely the opposite to how I saw it. I would congratulate people for having empty treatment rooms and applaud them for their work.

Treatment rooms are comfort areas that certain players would always gravitate to, to have a kiss and a cuddle if they are feeling sorry for themselves for not being in the team. That's one of the first things that has to change, because you cannot give your players any excuses or hiding places if they are not performing.

Similarly, I have always laughed at new managers who take over in mid-season and complain about the lack of fitness in their squad.

I am sure I have done it myself at some point, but then I had a reputation of managing extremely fit squads of players and it was always an area I studied really closely.

Early on in my management career, we weren't blessed with the advanced fitness equipment used in football today, but I was still able to quickly arrive at the level I believed the players should be at.

Firstly, I had my own fitness runs that were tried and tested but, also, I knew that if during a fitness session they weren't moaning and sweating, they weren't working hard enough.

Privately, you can realise very quickly when and which additions to the squad are needed.

Pochettino will no doubt be thinking about that at United already, but he has 10 games in the Premier League and Champions League before the January transfer window opens.

In the meantime, everything has to be geared towards winning games. I always knew I needed to do that quickly, because it helps the players believe in what I was doing, which is important too.

I've outlined my principles I held at every club above, and they never changed, but my playing principles were determined by the quality of the group I inherited.

My big strength as a coach was relaying what I needed from every individual player in the team, and I'm afraid repeated sessions were the go-to remedy to get there.

I apologise to all the lads who had to put up with me barking out the same commands, day after day, until even our weaker links would remember their individual and the team's plays in and out of possession.

The bottom of the Premier League table, before Saturday's results

It goes without saying that with United changing their manager again, their supporters will be hoping for an immediate bounce in respect of results and performance.

Michael Carrick's results when he took the reins at Old Trafford at the start of this year were fantastic, with six wins and a draw in his first seven league games - including victories over Manchester City and Arsenal .

As a consequence, he steered United from mid-table to third place and Champions League qualification.

Even if Pochettino delivers something similar then, for that success to last, he has to be able to have more control over the future recruitment into the club.

That has been an absolute disaster recently, and I don't believe blame for it can be thrown in Carrick's direction.

In fact, Pochettino should use what has happened as his argument for what needs to change to achieve his aims of bringing United out of recession and on the road to recovery.

Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The audio appeared to be coming from behind the judges during Saturday's episode (file photo)

The BBC has apologised "for any offence caused" after lewd audio was heard during the live broadcast of Strictly Come Dancing.

A recording of sex noises appeared to be playing from the audience in Blackpool's Tower Ballroom as judge Motsi Mabuse gave feedback early in Saturday's episode. She paused before joking: "It's not me."

At the end of the programme, presenter Emma Willis apologised to viewers "if you heard any audio disruptions". A BBC spokesperson also issued an apology and said it was "investigating how this happened".

Lancashire police said it was assessing whether any criminal offences may have taken place, after receiving a formal complaint and a mobile phone being seized.

The moment was streamed on social media by content creator Daniel Jarvis, whose videos include pranks. He appeared to place a phone call before the audio began playing in the ballroom, and suggested he was trying to target judge Craig Revel Horwood for his "bullying".

Jarvis has previously claimed he was responsible for sex noises disrupting Match of the Day in 2023 .

Willis told viewers: "Before we see the judges' leaderboard, we'd like to apologise if you heard any audio disruptions earlier in tonight's show and for any offence caused."

A BBC spokesperson said in a statement: "We apologise to any viewers offended during the live broadcast of Strictly this evening.

"We are investigating how this happened."

An edit will be made to the programme available on BBC iPlayer.

A spokesperson for Lancashire Constabulary said: "We are aware of an incident that took place during the filming of Strictly Come Dancing in Blackpool.

"We have been in contact with the event organisers, and a formal complaint has been made to us.

"A mobile phone has been seized and we are now looking into the matter to see if any criminal offences have taken place."

MN202611_1n53iebwev5.t:
I Am Helen charts a relationship spiralling after a non-consensual sexual experience

This article contains spoilers for I Am Helen

If you want to unwind on the sofa after a long day, I Am Helen probably isn't the show for you.

The Channel 4 drama starring Bridgerton star Nicola Coughlan and Joe Cole from Peaky Blinders has been called a must-watch by critics - but the cast don't want viewers sitting comfortably.

"There's going to be a few awkward sofas," Cole, who plays Helen's partner Steve, says.

"There's going to be people up and down the country that will be able to relate to this in varying degrees.

"And if we can put that in their living rooms and open up a debate, open up a conversation - and maybe help people be better - then we've done our job."

I Am Helen is the latest project in director Dominic Savage's I Am... series, female-led stories focusing on themes like mental health and relationships.

The two fully-improvised episodes, devised in collaboration with Coughlan, follow a relationship spiralling after Steve tries to choke Helen during sex without consent.

"We never realised how incredibly timely it would be," Coughlan tells BBC Newsbeat.

"It feels incredibly relevant right now, and specifically right now, because pornography that includes strangulation has just been outlawed in the UK."

Earlier this month, the government made it illegal for anyone to possess or publish porn that shows strangulation or suffocation.

That decision followed a review last year that found choking was "rife" on porn sites and had become normalised, particularly among younger people.

Coughlan and Cole say they were keen to make everything about their characters and the setting as relatable as possible to emphasise the shocking fallout.

"We needed one inciting incident that felt like something that could really plausibly happen between a couple, that it just goes slightly too far without consent, and it just blows everything up," Coughlan says.

"It's really important we see Steve's perspective in it because it makes him a normal guy.

"He's not this evil guy who's attacking Helen. He does bad things, but he's complicated. And hopefully you see them both as real people."

Bridgerton star Nicola Coughlan collaborated with director Dominic Savage on the drama

Filming the series without a script meant the actors were fully immersed in their characters, making them real not just for viewers but for themselves too.

"I'm not playing myself, but there's far less, let's say 'character' here than anything else I've ever done because a lot of this is about just reacting," Coughlan says.

She and Cole would film long takes, some lasting about an hour and often with heated exchanges, which might need to be shot multiple times.

Coughlan describes I Am Helen as "the most challenging thing in terms of material that I've ever worked on", adding for the first time in a role she needed counselling.

"You literally would be physically and mentally quite exhausted," she says.

"There were times that I said to Dominic [Savage] if he wanted to do a third take for example - and I've never said this before on set - but I actually don't think I have that in me because you hit a wall.

"When you're given that freedom, things happen and I think you can get some really interesting and also quite shocking stuff," he says.

For him, that came when he damaged a fridge on set with a punch.

But it's that authenticity of emotion which, while difficult for the actors, is what Coughlan thinks makes the series so engaging.

"When people watch the 'I Ams', they feel quite truthful," she says.

"I think that's a big reason as to why, to be honest."

Joe Cole and Nicola Coughlan wanted the fallout to feel plausible in a normal relationship

Cole researched the manosphere online while developing his role and says he could see how people like Steve "quickly become lost in this quite simple ideology".

"The more interesting thing was the lower level, the kind of 'bro influencer' type people, who a lot of what they say is actually quite good," he says.

"You know, 'go to the gym, be healthy, look your best'.

"But occasionally they veer into comments on male and female societal roles and how a woman should stay at home."

For someone like Steve, who Cole says wants a traditional relationship and a family, those ideas left him "completely lost".

The characters quickly "get caught in a cycle", he says, as they find it harder and harder to understand each other.

"It starts off as a question, which becomes a debate, which becomes an argument, which becomes a huge bust-up, which becomes forgiveness, an apology, tears."

Coughlan says viewers have told her they expected the series to end with serious violence, perhaps even with Steve killing Helen.

But she was determined to avoid a shock factor so the characters didn't tip into being unrelatable.

"There's some very extreme moments in this, but some of them are not extreme," she says.

"It's better that he didn't [kill Helen] because as a viewer, you don't want people to go, 'well, if he does X, then that's the moment to leave'.

"From my perspective, you watch it and you go, 'you don't need to hit a threshold'.

"If you feel scared and uncomfortable, that's enough reason to get out of a situation."

MP Sir Andrew Mitchell has campaigned for publicly accessible registers of who owns companies in British Overseas Territories and Crown Dependencies

Plans to improve transparency over company ownership in Guernsey and Jersey have come under criticism from a Westminster MP, who says they "do not go nearly far enough".

The comments come after Guernsey , external and Jersey , external set out plans to allow approved applicants access to information about who owns or controls companies when investigating suspected financial crime.

Sir Andrew Mitchell, who has campaigned for greater scrutiny of company ownership, said there were "immediate indications" the proposals would fall short.

He said limits on access to the information could mean "national security threats may remain entirely invisible to investigators".

The plans follow a joint commitment made by Guernsey, Jersey and the Isle of Man in December 2023 to increase transparency around company ownership and help tackle money laundering, terrorist financing and other financial crime.

Currently, information about who ultimately owns or controls companies is generally only available to law enforcement agencies, regulators and certain regulated businesses carrying out anti-money laundering checks.

The new proposals would allow journalists, academics and other applicants with a legitimate interest to apply for access.

Sir Andrew said investigators could face a "catch-22" because they may need access to the register to prove wrongdoing in the first place.

He also said he understood applicants would have to show they had been unable to find the information elsewhere, arguing: "This entirely defeats the object of a register."

Jersey's consultation response says applicants would be expected to show that "all reasonable alternative sources have been exhausted" before access was granted.

Guernsey's published response does not explicitly set out the same requirement.

He said: "Access should be open to those from other jurisdictions, for example those in the global south from whom much of the world's dirty money was stolen in the first place."

Sir Andrew also questioned whether users would have to pay to access the information, saying: "This information should be free at the point of access."

He said the proposals should eventually lead to fully public registers.

Both the governments of Guernsey and Jersey rejected Sir Andrew's criticism and said they continue to meet international standards in tackling financial crime.

A Government of Jersey spokesperson said the concerns raised by him "do not accurately reflect what is in Jersey's consultation response paper".

They said the policy was intended to help Jersey meet its international commitments while maintaining "a fair, proportionate, and effective transparency framework".

They added: "Jersey continues to meet international standards for transparency and countering money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing."

Deputy Andrew Niles, from Guernsey's Policy & Resources Committee, rejected Sir Andrew's criticism and pointed to a positive 2025 assessment of the island's efforts to tackle financial crime , external .

He said: "Guernsey does not accept the suggestion that our proposals fall short of the commitments we've made on beneficial ownership transparency or that the island does not meet international standards on beneficial ownership transparency."

He said the framework would provide access for people with a legitimate interest in investigating crime while protecting privacy and vulnerable individuals.

"The proposal is based on a tried and tested model adopted in the EU," he added.

MN202611_126o1cbfyqx.t:
Arsenal are six points behind third-placed London City Lionesses in the Women's Super League

Before the 2026-27 season began, Arsenal technical director Jodie Taylor declared: "I'll flat out say it: we want to win the league and want to take that next step."

After finishing second last season, it seemed like a logical statement to make.

However, after 10 games in this season's Women's Super League, they are sixth in the table, trailing leaders Chelsea by 13 points.

They are also nine points behind third-placed London City Lionesses, albeit with a game in hand, and facing stiff competition to qualify for the Champions League again next campaign.

BBC Sport looks at where things have gone wrong for the Gunners, who have not won the WSL since 2018-19.

Only bottom side Charlton have fewer home points than Arsenal this season

Last term, Arsenal hosted all 11 of their league home games at Emirates Stadium for the first time, winning eight times and drawing on three occasions.

This season, Renee Slegers' side have drawn all five of their home games and will seek their first win at the sixth attempt when they host West Ham on Sunday (14:30 GMT), live on BBC Two.

Two of those draws came against promoted sides Crystal Palace and Birmingham City, where a combined 57 shots yielded just one goal.

Home fans are getting disgruntled and this has been reflected in attendances. Last season, the Gunners had an average attendance of 33,808, better than eight Premier League clubs.

So far this year their biggest crowd was against London City Lionesses last weekend, when 32,588 were in the stands.

Speaking on the Women's Football Weekly podcast, former England striker Ellen White said: "The Emirates seems [like] a bit of an issue for them at the moment - they just can't get that win there.

"A draw might feel like a loss for them because they are so far behind now in terms of the Champions League spots."

Former Gunners striker Vivianne Miedema, who did play at Emirates Stadium for Arsenal but joined Manchester City before the full switch was made, added: "Players always say that the crowd really, really helps you at Arsenal. The fans are amazing - it gives you that extra bit of energy.

"Obviously playing in the Emirates with all the fans should still give them that boost but it doesn't seem to be fully working for them this season so far."

Alessia Russo has scored nine goals in all competitions for Arsenal this season

The Gunners have had 199 shots in 10 league matches but managed just 11 goals. That is just over one goal per game, and their conversion rate of 5.53% is the lowest of any club over the past six seasons.

Part of the problem could be an over-reliance on key goalscorer Alessia Russo.

She has alternated between the number nine and number 10 position during the season but thrives most when she is the focal point in the attack.

This season, the England striker has five league goals and provided two assists, with her form improving in recent weeks.

She was player of the match against Tottenham after scoring and providing an assist in a 2-1 win and similarly against Liverpool, when she scored twice to help Arsenal triumph by the same scoreline.

After Russo, only Lisa Baum (two), Georgia Stanway (two), Smilla Holmberg and Frida Maanum have scored in the league.

Injuries to attacking options Chloe Kelly, Selina Cerci and Stina Blackstenius have also proved costly, while key midfielder Mariona Caldentey is about halfway through an expected 10-week absence with a hamstring injury.

The result is that Arsenal and Brighton are the only teams in the league to have a goal difference of zero after 10 games.

Contrast that with title rivals Chelsea, who have scored 29 goals and have a goal difference of +24, while defending champions Manchester City have netted 27 times.

Slegers has been in charge of Arsenal since October 2024

While Slegers will always be hailed for winning Arsenal's second Champions League title last year against Barcelona, questions have been asked about her future after another slow start to the season.

In three of their home league matches, Arsenal have fallen behind and dropped points. Last Sunday, they went ahead against London City but only held the lead for 98 seconds.

It was a big summer of change in north London with club stalwarts Katie McCabe and Beth Mead among those departing, and seven new signings arriving including Stanway, Cerci and Baum.

Also among the arrivals was Swiss midfielder Geraldine Reuteler, who helped her country reach the quarter-finals of Euro 2025 but has struggled for minutes since signing a four-year deal in the summer.

She has made just four appearances across all competitions, appearing for a total of just 66 minutes in the WSL.

The results have left Slegers vulnerable and a first home win of the season against West Ham would be a much-needed boost for a side that have fallen far short of the lofty targets they set back in September.

MN202611_14nf0ls7x2m.t:
Harry Styles has carved out a solo career after One Direction

When Harry Styles was just 16, his mother Anne secretly signed up him up for the ITV's The X Factor talent show in the hope of turning his singing dreams into a reality.

Fast forward more than 15 years later and the 32-year-old is set for a prestigious headline slot at Glastonbury 2027.

Styles will perform on the Pyramid Stage alongside Sam Fender and Billie Eilish with Cher among the other stars on the bill.

But how exactly did Styles' career rocket from his early years growing up in the Cheshire village of Holmes Chapel to leading one of the most coveted festival sets in the music industry?

Styles attended Hermitage Primary School in his village, which lies just 25 miles (40km) south of Manchester.

His year two teacher Helen Bailey fondly remembers how the seven-year-old "always had a cheeky little smile on his face".

"I just remember him always being really happy, really smiley, really popular with his friends," said Helen, who has worked at the school for 26 years.

Her colleague Kathryn Davies, who taught Styles in year three, also remembers his "cheeky personality".

"He was a real pleasure to teach, you know, across all areas of the curriculum," she said.

"He did have a sense of humour, but he knew when to stop. He had perfect timing, so he never pushed it too far."

One of Styles' performances was filmed for a Netflix show One Night In Manchester

The signs were there from an early age with Styles taking on a number of roles in the school's shows, including the lead role of Barney the mouse in a nativity and a conductor in Bugsy Malone.

"He had what we thought at the time was quite a small part," said Kathryn.

"He was the conductor of the orchestra, but he just knew how to hold the audience.

"He just used to turn around and give a little wink without any training at all.

"This role of conductor - that we thought was quite a small part because he'd have his bigger part in year six - became a bigger part than we anticipated."

Styles loved performing from an early age

Both Helen and Kathryn said they went on to watch with pride as his career blossomed.

"We're proud obviously of all the children, but I think we did see a star in the making when he was at school," said Helen.

"We're super proud but it's quite surreal."

For Kathryn, she hopes his career acts as an inspiration to the future generations who attend the school.

"It's nice to see that somebody who starts off here and can become so successful," she said.

"Hopefully the children who are here will see that for themselves and think 'well anybody can live out their dream'."

Styles worked at a bakery in the village of Holmes Chapel while at school

Styles went on to attend Holmes Chapel Comprehensive School.

Earlier this year he gave out tickets to his sold-out Manchester show at the Co-op Live Arena to 50 pupils.

"As Harry's ex head teacher I am so pleased that he has kept a place in his heart for his roots and for the village and school where he grew and thrived," said Nigel Bielby at the time.

The village has since become no stranger to so-called "Harries" - as his fans are often dubbed - who travel to Cheshire to explore the place where their idol grew up.

Among the popular destinations is W. Mandeville's bakery, where Styles worked part-time while at school.

There is also a mural that depicts Styles and Cheshire's Twemlow Viaduct, where he reportedly had his first kiss.

This design, by local artists Victoria Holland and Eamonn Murphy, is a riff on popular vintage railway posters

In 2010, Styles travelled to his X Factor audition for his big break, earning a space in what would become the global phenomenon One Direction alongside Niall Horan, Liam Payne, Louis Tomlinson and Zayn Malik.

The boy band went on to release five albums in five years, dominating the music charts worldwide with their pop anthems.

With more than 200 million records sold worldwide, their music has received more than 21 billion streams across all platforms.

The band also won seven BRIT Awards, four MTV Music Awards, six Billboard Music Awards, seven American Music Awards and 28 Kids' Choice Awards.

One Direction quickly became a global success, performing around the world

Following the departure of Malik from the band in March 2015, the remaining members announced a break in order to pursue solo projects the following year.

Styles' debut solo single Sign of the Times was one of the most highly anticipated pop song of the year when it was released in 2017.

Since then he has released three albums in five years, with his fourth album Kiss All The Time, Disco Occasionally? put out earlier this year.

He has since received six Brit Awards, three Grammy Awards and two Ivor Novello Awards and enjoyed sold-out shows across the world.

Styles also turned his hand to acting with roles in Dunkirk, My Policeman and Don't Worry Darling.

Styles won Best Pop Vocal Album and Album of the Year for Harry's House in 2023

And there's more. Styles was awarded a Guinness World Record for the longest run of concerts at Wembley Stadium after completing 12 sold-out shows for the London leg of his Together, Together tour in June.

The star has broken the official record for the longest residency by a musician at the venue in a single run, beating Coldplay's previous record of 10 nights in 2025.

His mother wrote at the time: "From this to this… What a weekend! Hard to get my heart in check.

"From stating back in 1996 that my little boy would end up on stage, doing what I had no idea, but his comedic timing, sunshine personality, and his beautiful soul was visible even then.

"How could I have possibly known then that he would break records doing exactly what he was put in this world to do, that he would grow up being the kind of man the world needs right now."

Now her "little boy" is set to headline Glastonbury - a monumental moment for all musicians and, of course, for Harry's millions of fans.

MN202611_zqv73to3kn.t:
Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.

His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.

Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.

The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".

The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.

Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.

Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.

The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.

The business broke into luxury markets and diversified beyond jewellery into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels.

"Paolo Bulgari began collaborating with his father in 1960, specialising in the knowledge of precious stones, of which he was one of the world's leading experts, and refining the sensibility and aesthetic sense that are at the root of the Bvlgari style," the Bvlgari company posted on social media. , external

"He poured his heart into his craft and into nurturing the talents of young designers, leaving an indelible mark on the world of jewellery.

"Thank you, Mr. Paolo, your legacy as a brilliant beacon of creative inspiration will continue to inspire generations to come."

Paolo Bulgari alongside David Bowie and his wife Iman in September 1991 in Versailles, France.

The post included a quote from Paolo Bulgari: "Everything can be a source of inspiration. There are no rules in creativity. Never."

The designer brand's celebrity clients have included Elizabeth Taylor, Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe, Ingrid Bergman, Sophie Loren, Anne Hathaway, Zendaya and Rihanna.

Actor Zendaya wearing a Bvlgari necklace at the 2025 Golden Globe awards.

In 2011 the family sold its controlling stake to the French luxury group LVMH, in a deal worth about 3.7 billion euros.

In 2019, he and his wife established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation to support young people through schooling and job training in disadvantaged neighbourhoods on the outskirts of Rome.

The funeral will take place in Rome on Monday, 23 November in the Basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.

MN202611_fpbi2y4ejs.t:
Umukuru w'abacuruza ibiyobyabwenge wari uri ku rutonde rw'abantu 10 bashakishwa cyane n'urwego rw'ubugenzacyaha rw'Amerika (FBI) yatawe muri yombi nyuma yo kurasana n'abasirikare ba Mexique.

Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores n'abandi bantu barindwi bafashwe ku wa gatanu n'umutwe wihariye wo mu ngabo za Mexique, mu mujyi wa Guasave, muri leta ya Sinaloa, nkuko bitangazwa na minisiteri y'ingabo za Mexique.

Iyo minisiteri yongeyeho ko abacyekwa barindwi biciwe muri icyo gikorwa cya gisirikare, ndetse n'abasirikare bane ba Mexique, bari barimo kujya gukaza umutekano i Guasave, na bo bishwe.

Meza Flores yashakishwaga muri Mexique kubera ibirego by'ubugizi bwa nabi buteguwe, mu gihe FBI imushinja "kurunda muri Amerika [ibiyobyabwenge bya] fentanyl, cocaine, heroin n'ibindi biyobyabwenge byica". Amerika irimo gushaka ko yoherezwayo.

Mexique yongereye ibikorwa byo kurwanya ubugizi bwa nabi bushingiye ku biyobyabwenge, nyuma yuko yocyejwe igitutu na Perezida w'Amerika Donald Trump kuva asubiye ku butegetsi mu mwaka ushize.

Meza Flores, umukuru w'igico cyitwa 'Meza Flores Organisation', kinazwi nka 'Guasave Cartel', byibazwa ko yatangiye gucuruza ibiyobyabwenge kuva mu myaka ya 1990 ariko yari yarashoboye kugenda akwepa abategetsi, kugeza ubwo yafatwaga ku wa gatanu, akaba yari yarabishoboye kubera ko muri rusange atigaragazaga mu ruhame nk'umuntu ukomeye.

Bashingiye ku makuru y'ubutasi bahawe n'Amerika ajyanye n'ahantu yari aherereye, abasirikare bo mu mutwe wihariye wo mu ngabo za Mexique berekejeyo "bucece kandi mu buryo butunguranye", bashyiraho uruzitiro rwo kumubuza gutoroka no gutuma hataza abo kumutabara, nkuko bivugwa na minisiteri y'ingabo za Mexique.

Iyo minisiteri yongeyeho ko ariko abo basirikare "bagabweho igitero cy'amasasu n'ibiturika" mbere yuko binjira aho hantu, nuko bata muri yombi Meza Flores.

Videwo zahererekanyijwe ku mbuga zo kuri murandasi (internet) uko bigaragara zerekana indege za kajugujugu zirimo kurasa urufaya rw'amasasu ku butaka i Guasave. Izindi videwo, uko bigaragara, zerekana abantu bari mu kibuga cy'umukino wa baseball barimo guhunga ubwo bumvaga urusaku rw'amasasu.

Bose hamwe, abantu umunani batawe muri yombi, barimo uwungirije Meza Flores akaba ari na mubyara we, muramu we, uyu akaba ari na we wari ushinzwe imari muri icyo gico, nkuko minisiteri y'ingabo yabivuze.

Meza Flores, mubyara we na muramu we bajyanwe n'indege mu mujyi wa Mexico, umurwa mukuru wa Mexique, kugira ngo baburanishwe, nkuko minisiteri y'ingabo yabivuze. Abo bandi batanu bagumishijwe muri leta ya Sinaloa.

Mu mwaka wa 2025, ubwo Meza Flores yongerwaga ku rutonde rwa FBI rw'abantu ishakisha cyane, yashinjwaga "ibyaha ndengakamere" birimo ubushimusi, ubwambuzi n'iyicarubozo.

Icyo gihe, uwari umuyobozi w'agateganyo wa FBI, Brian Driscoll, yavuze ko Meza Flores n'igico cye banateje muri Amerika "icyago cy'ibiyobyabwenge binyuranyije n'amategeko" binyuze ku mupaka wayo wo mu majyepfo ihana na Mexique.

Mbere, yarezwe ubucuruzi bw'ibiyobyabwenge muri Amerika mu mwaka wa 2012, yongera kuregwa mu mwaka wa 2019.

Meza Flores, w'imyaka 44, ashinjwa kuba yaracuze umugambi wo gukora no gukwirakwiza ibiyobyabwenge byinshi bya cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine n'urumogi hagati y'umwaka wa 2005 n'uwa 2019.

MN202611_hyr58ik1pc.t:
Midwife turnover in the Welsh NHS is at its lowest level for over 16 years

Midwives who will graduate in Wales next year have been told there are fewer jobs available for them than expected.

The Royal College of Midwives said this is in addition to the 66 newly qualified midwives who didn't manage to find a job after they graduated last year.

Director of RCM Cymru Julie Richards said the situation was "unacceptable" when maternity services are "facing pressure from every direction" .

The Welsh government said it recognised the concerns around employment uncertainty and it was working with NHS Wales "to understand workforce pressures and requirements".

Kimmy Williams, 37, from Swansea has had to return to her old job working in the kitchen at a local college because there aren't enough midwifery graduate jobs available in Wales.

Williams said she's aware that almost half of her peers on the midwifery course at Swansea University are yet to find a job despite the promise of employment for everyone once they graduated.

Her dream job was to become a midwife after having children of her own 16 years ago, but she has instead been left with "a mountain of debt and no job at the end of it".

"Now I'm just working in the same job I was previously but worse off financially," she added.

Williams said she would accept minimum wage to do the job initially just to be able to get into the system and progress her career.

Almost half of people on Kimmy Williams' midwifery course are yet to find a job

The Royal College of Midwives said students across Wales are facing the same "deepening crisis".

Megan Lewis, from Cardiff, said it's hard to understand why so many newly qualified midwives in Wales, like her, are not able to get a job after witnessing first hand how "stretched" services can become.

"Midwives regularly told us how much they valued having students on shift because we were another pair of hands to help with care," she said.

Midwifery students have their tuition fees paid by NHS Wales on the condition they commit to working in the country for up to two years after they graduate.

Although a number of jobs may come up at some health boards, RCM Cymru said it had not been confirmed how many vacancies will become available, but they were "challenging the suggestion that improved retention is behind the lack of jobs for newly qualified midwives in Wales".

Richards said RCM Cymru's members had told them they were working "under enormous pressure".

"They are working above their contracted hours, they're missing breaks, many are having their training cancelled," she added.

"Quite clearly there is a need for these graduate midwives to enter into the workforce now."

Health Education and Improvement Wales (HEIW) said the NHS would not be running a national recruitment round in spring 2027 as "very few roles" are expected to become available.

HEIW said midwife turnover in NHS Wales is at its lowest level for over 16 years meaning "fewer roles have become available than expected".

It also said financial pressures have limited the number of Band 5 roles health boards can offer to newly qualified midwives.

Chief executive Alex Howells said HEIW was "working with health boards to establish what roles they can offer and how graduates can apply."

Joseph Langdon was supported by the Bristol Old Vic while in a young offenders' institute

A former young offender who became a West End actor says taking drama lessons while he was detained was the best decision he ever made.

Joseph Langdon, who grew up in south London, was convicted of gang-related crimes at the the age of 16. But while in a young offenders' institute, he was offered drama lessons through a scheme with the Bristol Old Vic.

Langdon said the lessons taught him "that I could make something of my life, and introduced me to this world I did not think was possible".

The actor, who will play the prince in the theatre's Christmas production of Cinderella: A Fairytale, said: "I count my blessings every day. I turn up to rehearsals with a huge smile on my face."

"I'm now working all over the world and have the most amazing life," he added.

"When I think of old friends from when I was a kid – some are dead now, some are in prison and I know that would be my life if it wasn't for Bristol Old Vic giving me a chance and hope."

'I focused on getting a baby, not what came next'

From young offender to Bristol Panto star

While in a young offenders' institute in Bristol, he was taught drama every week through a scheme run by the Bristol Old Vic Young Company.

"At first I was like, 'No I'm not going to go, I feel a bit too cool for this'.

"But when I did decide to go it was the best decision I ever made. I never skipped a lesson," he said.

At the end of his sentence, Langdon was told he could either move back to London and "get caught up in the same trouble" or move to Bristol "and start life afresh".

The cast of Cinderella have been rehearsing at the Bristol Old Vic

Langdon moved to Bristol, where he lived in youth hostels and halfway houses while training at the Old Vic through the Made in Bristol scheme - a free programme for young theatre makers.

He said coming out of prison was tough, but his support network kept him "on track".

The actor also worked at the theatre's box office and took part in various productions before returning to south London to study at Mountview drama school, thanks to a bursary scheme.

He said he was anxious about going back to the area he grew up in but "everybody was so supportive and proud".

After graduating, Langdon went on to act in numerous films and productions, including in the West End.

"Being adopted by Bristol has been the biggest blessing of my life," said Langdon, who returns to the city to star in Cinderella.

"The Bristol Old Vic has such a special, special, magical energy" and it is "truly an honour and a blessing to be part of that," said the actor.

Lucy Hunt, Bristol Old Vic's director of engagement, said Langdon understood "first-hand how a bit of belief in a young person can make a big impact on their lives".

"I am so happy he is back," said Hunt. "He is the best positive energy to have around and he's going to be amazing as the prince."

Langdon says he pinches himself every day

The Olivier Award-nominated adaptation of Cinderella was devised by Bristol artists Sally Cookson, Adam Peck and the Original Company and draws from various versions of the fairytale, including the Brothers Grimm story.

"Ultimately, it's a beautiful family show full of fun, magic and wonder," said Langdon.

Langdon now goes into schools and gives talks to "be that representation" for those interested in theatre.

He says he wants to "show other people from all different backgrounds, no matter who you are, that this is possible".

Cinderella: A Fairytale runs at the Bristol Old Vic from 27 November to 2 January.
